name: Zoe Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. So you can tell me the public version and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Larkspur Accounting, twelve of us in an old mill building by the river. We specialise in online sellers, people who sell candles or phone cases or vintage clothes through the big marketplace sites. Their accounts are a mess of platform fees, refunds and sales in five currencies, and I untangle it into a tax return. I use AI all day. I wrote the firm's one-page guide on how to use it safely, which my boss Nadia printed and stuck by the kettle.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sam, who's a freelance graphic designer. Sam's work has dropped by about a third this year because clients are making their own logos with AI image tools, so we're living mostly on my pay, which isn't great for this job. We've got about three weeks' money in the bank. There are only a couple of firms like ours within an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are good at the boring stuff and that's fine. At work I'd keep pushing the useful bits, like reconciling platform payouts, and drop the hype. Online I'd post a calm thread about what actually saved time and what didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI flopping wouldn't fix my real problem, which is that my partner Sam's design work has already dried up. Image tools have hit Sam even if the big stuff never comes. So we'd still be one income and a bit, on a lower-paid accountant's salary, in a town with two other firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep automating the dull parts so I can take on a few more clients and ask Nadia for a bonus tied to it. I'd help Sam pitch to local businesses who still want a human designer. And we'd keep a tight budget, no holiday this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about my own job, really, but about the two of us together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did Sam take the drop in work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. Sam spent a week refreshing their email waiting for a client who'd gone quiet. Now they're more practical about it, doing menus and signs for cafés who want someone they can meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Nadia give you that bonus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small one. Nadia likes that I'm the AI person, but she also likes saving money. I'd show her the hours saved in a spreadsheet, because Nadia only believes numbers.

She'd post a calm thread on what **actually saved time**.
think: AI flopping doesn't help, because **Sam's design work** has already dropped.
They're living on **one income** and a bit in a town with few firms.
do: Automate dull tasks and ask Nadia for a **bonus** tied to it.
Help Sam pitch to **local businesses** wanting a human designer.
Keep a **tight budget** and skip a holiday this year.
feel: Uneasy, less about her job than about the **two of them**.

She shows **Sam** as the earner already hit by AI image tools.

steps.text: Automate platform payout reconciliations for more online-seller clients
Help Sam pitch design work to local cafés and shops
Skip a holiday this year and keep a tight budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms that adapt will be fine and the ones that don't won't be around. I'd be honest at work that some roles will shrink, including some of mine. Online I'd share how we're changing, because people want real examples, not hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm on the right side of it for a few years, because I'm the one setting it up. But the routine returns we do would need two people, not five. If I'm not careful, I automate myself into a smaller team that doesn't need me either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Nadia to make me the lead on rolling out the tools, with a title and a bit more pay. I'd start an online course in finance systems, the software side of accounting, in the evenings. And I'd put any extra pay straight into savings, because Sam's income is so up and down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and excited at the same time. I like change, but I can't afford to be wrong about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Larkspur would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, who's forty-five and does the routine returns. Danny's careful and slow and always right. In this picture careful and slow isn't valued anymore, and I'd feel awful about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worst case for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia decides an outside software firm can do the rollout better and cheaper. Then I'm just another accountant, on lower pay, with skills that everyone else is catching up on. That's the version that worries me.

S1.quote: If I'm not careful, I automate myself into a smaller team that doesn't need me either.
fieldNote: Zoe sees her edge as **temporary**, so even as the AI person she's anxious.
Her worst case is an **outside firm** doing the rollout instead of her.
She worries for **Danny**, a careful older colleague whose strengths lose value.

steps.text: Lead Larkspur's AI rollout with a new title and pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a serious national plan, not slogans, and fast. I'd be practical online: here's what's changing, here's who to call. At work I'd tell Nadia straight that the firm as we know it has two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means my job goes, and so does Sam's, because design is thinking work too. My whole job is screen work, so I don't even get the three extra years the hands-on people get. Being early with AI just means I see my job going more clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year earning everything I can helping other small firms switch to AI, because for about eighteen months that's a real job. I'd save every spare penny into a separate account. And I'd talk to Sam about whether Sam's parents would let us live in their annexe while we work out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time I've imagined both of us losing work at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're a team and we'll be a team with no money if we have to be. Then I'd probably open a spreadsheet, because that's how I cope. Sam would make tea and draw something, which is how Sam copes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: After the eighteen months of helping firms switch, then what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe something hands-on until 2031, or something where people want a human face. That's the part I can't plan yet, and I'm a planner.

fieldNote: Zoe expects to lose her job and **Sam's income** too, so alarmed fits.
She'd use a short **switching window** to earn while it lasts.

steps.text: Help small firms switch to AI on paid contracts for eighteen months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if people stop pretending it isn't happening. I'd post practical guides and maybe run a local session for small business owners. At work I'd lay out a plan for Larkspur, year by year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is a decent window. I'd ride the AI rollout work for three years and earn more than I ever have. Then I'd need something else by 2031, ideally with people at the centre of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd become the rollout lead at Larkspur and pick up freelance setup work for other firms. I'd save at least three hundred a month from that. And I'd start a part-time course in business coaching or mediation, something where a person in the room still matters after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. I'd have a plan on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Sam do in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would have time too. We've talked about Sam training as a sign maker, the physical kind, routing and fitting shop signs, which is hands-on until about 2034. It's a weird pairing, but it might work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd earn more than ever. Is that comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. It's good money for helping the change happen, and I'd know it's the same change that ends my job. I'd take the money anyway, because savings are the only thing that buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if you start early, and most people won't. I'd be the one at work making the plan and online sharing it. I'd also tell friends not to panic, because ten years is a whole career for some people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it's fine. I'd be thirty-seven, with years of running AI systems behind me. I'd have time to save, move into a people-based role and help Sam find steadier work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, lead the rollout, and build a small consultancy on the side over three or four years. I'd save steadily, five percent at first, more as the side work grows. And Sam and I would finally plan the wedding, small, in 2028, because ten years feels like room to live normally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at most. It's the version where my curiosity actually pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still keep you up at night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam. Sam's work is already shrinking now, before any of this. If Sam's still struggling in five years, my plan has to carry two people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the wedding happen in this picture and not the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in the others I'd be spending the wedding money on rent. Ten years gives you room to do the normal things too. Ten years is the only picture where I'd say yes to a wedding date with my partner Sam.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes both of us at once and leaves no time to plan. What would help is a guaranteed income for a year or two while people retrain, and help for freelancers like Sam, who fall through every gap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about freelancers. Everyone talks about employees being let go. Freelancers like my partner Sam just stop getting emails, and nobody counts them as losing a job.

headlineQuote: Freelancers like my partner Sam just stop getting emails, and nobody counts them as losing a job.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old** accountant at a twelve-person firm serving **online sellers**.
She uses AI daily and wrote the firm's **guide** on using it safely.
She lives with Sam, a freelance designer whose work has **already dropped**, on about three weeks' savings.
She plans to **earn from the rollout** first, then move into people-based work.
She runs from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, and is easiest with ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would take her job and Sam's work at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** during retraining and help for **freelancers**.
